Guideline: Pin One Version and Load ES Modules
Description: The manual recommends npm plus a build tool for most projects. Without a build step, load three.js as ES modules through an import map that maps 'three' to build/three.module.js and 'three/addons/' to examples/jsm/ of the same pinned version on the same CDN. The classic build/three.min.js global script was removed in r161, so current releases have no window.THREE global; mixing versions or CDNs can include duplicate code or break at runtime.
Do: Pin an exact version in both import-map entries (or in package.json) and import everything from that one source
Don't: Use an unversioned or latest URL, the removed build/three.min.js global script, or files from different versions or CDNs
Code Good: <script type="importmap">{ "imports": { "three": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@<version>/build/three.module.js", "three/addons/": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@<version>/examples/jsm/" } }</script> <script type="module">import * as THREE from 'three';</script>
Code Bad: <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three/build/three.min.js"></script> <!-- unpinned; global build removed in r161 -->

Description: Controls, loaders and post-processing are addons: they ship in the package but are not part of the core namespace, so THREE.OrbitControls and THREE.GLTFLoader are undefined. Import them from 'three/addons/...'. The legacy examples/js scripts that attached addons to THREE were removed in r148.
Do: Import each addon module from 'three/addons/' using the same version as core
Don't: Call new THREE.OrbitControls() or load addon scripts from the removed examples/js directory
Code Good: import { OrbitControls } from 'three/addons/controls/OrbitControls.js'; const controls = new OrbitControls(camera, renderer.domElement);
Code Bad: const controls = new THREE.OrbitControls(camera, renderer.domElement); // TypeError: not a constructor

Guideline: Check Snippets Against the Installed Revision
Description: three.js does not follow semver: any rNNN release can rename or remove APIs, and older tutorials reproduce them. Examples: THREE.Geometry was removed from core in r125, outputEncoding/sRGBEncoding were replaced in r152, CapsuleGeometry's length parameter became height in r176, and Clock was deprecated in r183. Read the installed revision and check the migration guide entries after the snippet's revision.
Do: Check the installed version and the migration guide before reusing code written for an older revision
Don't: Paste tutorial code without checking it for removed or renamed APIs
Code Good: const geo = new THREE.BufferGeometry(); geo.setAttribute('position', new THREE.BufferAttribute(new Float32Array(vertices), 3));
Code Bad: const geo = new THREE.Geometry(); geo.vertices.push(new THREE.Vector3(0, 0, 0)); // removed from core in r125

Guideline: One Renderer Per Canvas and Dispose It
Description: Each WebGLRenderer owns a WebGL context. Create it once per canvas and reuse it while the canvas lives; recreating renderers on every mount or scene change accumulates contexts and GPU resources. Call renderer.dispose() when the canvas is torn down.
Do: Create the renderer once, swap scene content, and call renderer.dispose() on teardown
Don't: Construct a new renderer on every component mount or scene transition without disposing the old one
Code Good: const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ canvas }); // reuse for the canvas lifetime; on teardown: renderer.setAnimationLoop(null); renderer.dispose();
Code Bad: function showScene() { const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer(); document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement); } // new context on every call

Description: With alpha: true the renderer's default clear alpha is 0, so page content behind the canvas shows through. Without it the clear alpha is 1 and the canvas covers what is behind it. Decide this at construction; the visible background can then come from CSS or scene.background.
Do: Pass alpha: true when the canvas must composite over HTML behind it
Don't: Expect an opaque default renderer to reveal the page behind the canvas
Code Good: const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ alpha: true }); // default clear alpha is 0
Code Bad: const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer(); // clear alpha 1: the canvas hides the HTML behind it

Guideline: Resize From the Canvas and Update the Projection
Description: Size the drawing buffer from the canvas's displayed size (clientWidth/clientHeight), not the window, and on every size change update camera.aspect, call camera.updateProjectionMatrix(), and call renderer.setSize(width, height, false). Passing false stops setSize from writing inline styles so CSS keeps control of layout. A ResizeObserver also catches container-only size changes that the window resize event misses.
Do: Observe the canvas size; update aspect, updateProjectionMatrix() and setSize(w, h, false) together
Don't: Size from window.innerWidth/innerHeight for a canvas inside a container, or leave the aspect ratio stale
Code Good: const ro = new ResizeObserver(() => { const w = canvas.clientWidth, h = canvas.clientHeight; renderer.setSize(w, h, false); camera.aspect = w / h; camera.updateProjectionMatrix(); }); ro.observe(canvas);
Code Bad: window.addEventListener('resize', () => renderer.setSize(window.innerWidth, window.innerHeight)); // aspect never updated; ignores container size

Guideline: Move the Camera Off the Origin
Description: Objects added to a scene are placed at (0, 0, 0), and so is a new camera, so the camera starts inside the object. Set an explicit camera position (and lookAt if needed) before the first render.
Do: Set camera.position and, where needed, camera.lookAt() before the first render
Don't: Render with the camera left at the origin inside the subject
Code Good: camera.position.set(0, 1.5, 5); camera.lookAt(new THREE.Vector3(0, 0, 0));
Code Bad: // camera and subject both at (0, 0, 0) — the subject is not visible

Guideline: Create Geometry Once and Mutate Attributes
Description: Constructing geometry inside the render loop allocates new GPU buffers every frame, and they are not freed without dispose(). Create geometry once before the loop; if vertices must change, mutate the existing BufferAttribute and flag it for upload.
Do: Create geometry before the loop; mutate BufferAttribute arrays in place when shapes change
Don't: Call any new XxxGeometry() constructor inside the animation loop
Code Good: const geo = new THREE.SphereGeometry(1, 32, 16); const mesh = new THREE.Mesh(geo, mat); scene.add(mesh); renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => renderer.render(scene, camera));
Code Bad: renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => { const geo = new THREE.BoxGeometry(1, 1, 1); /* new GPU buffers every frame */ renderer.render(scene, camera); });

Description: Meshes with the same shape or appearance can reference the same geometry and material instances while keeping their own transforms. Duplicates multiply GPU buffers, programs and dispose work. Dispose shared resources only when no mesh uses them any more.
Do: Create one geometry and one material and pass the same references to every matching Mesh
Don't: Create an identical geometry or material inside a loop for each object
Code Good: const geo = new THREE.BoxGeometry(1, 1, 1); const mat = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial(); for (const p of positions) { const m = new THREE.Mesh(geo, mat); m.position.copy(p); scene.add(m); }
Code Bad: for (const p of positions) scene.add(new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.BoxGeometry(1, 1, 1), new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial())); // one buffer and material per mesh

Description: three.js does not release GPU resources automatically. When an object leaves the app, call dispose() on its geometry, materials, textures and render targets (shared ones only when their last user is gone); addons such as controls also expose dispose(). renderer.info reports live geometry and texture counts for checking leaks.
Do: Dispose geometry, material, every texture map and addon instances when they are no longer used
Don't: Call scene.remove() alone and assume memory is reclaimed
Code Good: scene.remove(mesh); mesh.geometry.dispose(); mesh.material.map?.dispose(); mesh.material.normalMap?.dispose(); mesh.material.dispose(); controls.dispose();
Code Bad: scene.remove(mesh); // geometry, textures and programs stay allocated

Description: MeshBasicMaterial is not affected by lights, so adding lights for it changes nothing. Lit materials (Lambert, Phong, Standard, Physical) respond to lights and environment maps. Choose by whether the surface should respond to lighting.
Do: Use MeshBasicMaterial for surfaces that must not react to lighting; use a lit material for surfaces that should
Don't: Add lights expecting them to change MeshBasicMaterial surfaces
Code Good: const label = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ map: labelTexture }); // unlit: no lights needed for this surface
Code Bad: scene.add(new THREE.AmbientLight()); // added only for MeshBasicMaterial objects — no visible effect

Guideline: Lit Materials Need a Light or Environment
Description: MeshStandardMaterial, MeshPhysicalMaterial and the other lit materials render black when the scene has no lights and no environment map. Add at least one light, or set scene.environment, which applies to all physical materials in the scene.
Do: Add a light or assign scene.environment whenever lit materials are used
Don't: Use lit materials in a scene with no lights and no environment map
Code Good: const light = new THREE.DirectionalLight(); light.position.set(1, 2, 3); scene.add(light); // or: scene.environment = envTexture;
Code Bad: scene.add(new THREE.Mesh(geo, new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial())); // no light and no environment — renders black

Description: WebGLRenderer.useLegacyLights became false by default and deprecated in r155 and is absent from current releases, so lighting uses physically based units. Light intensities copied from pre-r155 examples render differently; re-tune intensities for the installed revision instead of reviving legacy mode. Point and spot light decay has defaulted to the physical value 2 since r147.
Do: Tune light intensities against the installed revision
Don't: Copy intensity values from pre-r155 examples or set renderer.useLegacyLights
Code Good: const lamp = new THREE.PointLight(); lamp.intensity = lampIntensity; // value tuned for r155+ physical units
Code Bad: renderer.useLegacyLights = true; // deprecated in r155; not part of current WebGLRenderer

Guideline: Shadows Need Renderer, Light and Mesh Flags
Description: Shadows render only when renderer.shadowMap.enabled is true, the light has castShadow, casters have castShadow and receivers have receiveShadow (both default to false). For every shadow-casting light, all casters are rendered again from that light's point of view, so enable the flags only where shadows matter. PCFSoftShadowMap is deprecated for WebGLRenderer since r182 because PCFShadowMap is now soft.
Do: Enable renderer.shadowMap, then castShadow/receiveShadow only on the lights and meshes that need them
Don't: Set castShadow without enabling renderer.shadowMap, or flag every object and light
Code Good: renderer.shadowMap.enabled = true; light.castShadow = true; hero.castShadow = true; ground.receiveShadow = true;
Code Bad: light.castShadow = true; hero.castShadow = true; // renderer.shadowMap.enabled never set — no shadows

Guideline: Reuse One Raycaster and Set the Ray First
Description: Create one Raycaster and one pointer Vector2 and reuse them. Call raycaster.setFromCamera(pointer, camera) before intersectObjects whenever the pointer or camera has moved. intersectObject(s) has been recursive by default since r133, so groups and loaded models are tested through their descendants.
Do: Reuse one Raycaster; call setFromCamera before every intersectObjects
Don't: Allocate a Raycaster per event or intersect without updating the ray
Code Good: const raycaster = new THREE.Raycaster(); const pointer = new THREE.Vector2(); function pick(targets) { raycaster.setFromCamera(pointer, camera); return raycaster.intersectObjects(targets); }
Code Bad: canvas.addEventListener('pointermove', () => { const rc = new THREE.Raycaster(); rc.intersectObjects(targets); }); // new instance per event; ray never set

Guideline: Pointer to NDC From the Canvas Rectangle
Description: setFromCamera expects normalized device coordinates: x from -1 (left) to 1 (right) and y from 1 (top) to -1 (bottom). Compute them relative to canvas.getBoundingClientRect() so offset or non-fullscreen canvases map correctly, and negate y.
Do: Derive NDC from the canvas bounding rect and invert the y axis
Don't: Use window size for a non-fullscreen canvas or forget to negate y
Code Good: const r = canvas.getBoundingClientRect(); pointer.x = ((e.clientX - r.left) / r.width) * 2 - 1; pointer.y = -((e.clientY - r.top) / r.height) * 2 + 1;
Code Bad: pointer.x = (e.clientX / window.innerWidth) * 2 - 1; pointer.y = (e.clientY / window.innerHeight) * 2 - 1; // ignores canvas offset; y not inverted

Description: The renderer docs advise defining the animation loop with renderer.setAnimationLoop(callback) rather than manual requestAnimationFrame. WebXR projects use it, and WebGPURenderer guarantees initialization inside it. Pass null to stop the loop. Timers such as setInterval are not synchronized with display refresh.
Do: Use renderer.setAnimationLoop(callback) and pass null to stop it
Don't: Drive rendering with setInterval or setTimeout
Code Good: renderer.setAnimationLoop((time) => { timer.update(time); renderer.render(scene, camera); }); // stop: renderer.setAnimationLoop(null);
Code Bad: setInterval(() => renderer.render(scene, camera), 16); // not synchronized with the display

Description: Scale motion by elapsed time, not per-frame constants that change speed with refresh rate. Clock is deprecated since r183; use THREE.Timer (in core since r179). Call timer.update(timestamp) once per frame, then getDelta() and getElapsed() return the same values for that frame however often they are read. timer.connect(document) uses the Page Visibility API to avoid a large delta after the tab was hidden.
Do: Call timer.update() once per frame and scale motion by timer.getDelta()
Don't: Use the deprecated Clock or fixed per-frame increments
Code Good: const timer = new THREE.Timer(); timer.connect(document); renderer.setAnimationLoop((t) => { timer.update(t); mesh.rotation.y += timer.getDelta() * speed; renderer.render(scene, camera); });
Code Bad: renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => { mesh.rotation.y += 0.01; renderer.render(scene, camera); }); // speed depends on refresh rate

Description: Material.opacity only takes effect when material.transparent is true; otherwise the material stays fully opaque. Transparent objects need special handling and are rendered after opaque ones, so enable it only where needed.
Do: Set transparent: true on any material whose opacity is below 1 or is animated
Don't: Change opacity on a material with transparent left false
Code Good: const mat = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ transparent: true, opacity: 0.5 });
Code Bad: const mat = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ opacity: 0.5 }); // transparent false — still fully opaque

Description: InstancedMesh renders many objects that share geometry and material but differ in transform with fewer draw calls. After setMatrixAt (or setColorAt) set the matching needsUpdate flag so the instance data is uploaded.
Do: Use InstancedMesh when many objects share geometry and material; flag instanceMatrix.needsUpdate after edits
Don't: Add a separate Mesh for each of many identical objects
Code Good: const mesh = new THREE.InstancedMesh(geo, mat, count); const m = new THREE.Matrix4(); for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) { m.setPosition(xs[i], ys[i], zs[i]); mesh.setMatrixAt(i, m); } mesh.instanceMatrix.needsUpdate = true; scene.add(mesh);
Code Bad: for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) scene.add(new THREE.Mesh(geo, mat)); // one draw call per object

Description: In r152 outputEncoding/sRGBEncoding were replaced by outputColorSpace/SRGBColorSpace and Texture.encoding by Texture.colorSpace; the old names are absent from current releases. ColorManagement is enabled by default and outputColorSpace defaults to SRGBColorSpace. Mark color textures (albedo, emissive) as SRGBColorSpace and leave data textures such as normal or roughness maps at NoColorSpace. Tone mapping defaults to NoToneMapping; choosing an operator is a separate look decision.
Do: Set texture.colorSpace = THREE.SRGBColorSpace on color textures and keep data textures at NoColorSpace
Don't: Use outputEncoding, sRGBEncoding or texture.encoding
Code Good: const tex = await new THREE.TextureLoader().loadAsync('albedo.jpg'); tex.colorSpace = THREE.SRGBColorSpace; material.map = tex; // renderer.outputColorSpace defaults to SRGBColorSpace
Code Bad: renderer.outputEncoding = THREE.sRGBEncoding; tex.encoding = THREE.sRGBEncoding; // pre-r152 API

Description: antialias selects the WebGL context's default MSAA and can only be passed to the WebGLRenderer constructor; assigning it afterwards has no effect because the context already exists.
Do: Set antialias:true inside the WebGLRenderer constructor options object
Don't: Construct the renderer without antialias then try to enable it by assigning the property
Code Good: const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: true, alpha: true }); // antialias baked into the WebGL context
Code Bad: const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer(); renderer.antialias = true; // no effect — context created without AA — edges remain aliased

Description: Render a particle field as one Points object over a BufferGeometry position attribute instead of one Mesh per particle; each Mesh is a separate draw call.
Do: Use Points with a BufferGeometry position attribute for particle effects
Don't: Create one Mesh per particle
Code Good: const pos = new Float32Array(count * 3); /* fill */ const geo = new THREE.BufferGeometry(); geo.setAttribute('position', new THREE.BufferAttribute(pos, 3)); scene.add(new THREE.Points(geo, new THREE.PointsMaterial({ size: 0.05 })));
Code Bad: for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) scene.add(new THREE.Mesh(sphereGeo, mat)); // one draw call per particle

Description: After changing a BufferAttribute's array, set attribute.needsUpdate = true so the data is re-sent to the GPU; otherwise the GPU keeps rendering the old values.
Do: Set needsUpdate = true on the position attribute after every per-frame mutation of the array
Don't: Mutate the Float32Array values without flagging needsUpdate — positions update in JS but not on the GPU
Code Good: const pos = geo.attributes.position; for (let i = 0; i < pos.count; i++) pos.setY(i, pos.getY(i) + dt * speed); pos.needsUpdate = true;
Code Bad: geo.attributes.position.array[1] += 0.001; // needsUpdate not set — GPU copy is stale

Guideline: Pointer Events for Mouse, Touch and Pen
Description: Pointer Events (pointerdown, pointermove, pointerup) give mouse, touch and pen one code path. When the scene consumes drag gestures, set the CSS touch-action property on the canvas so the browser does not also pan or zoom the page.
Do: Listen for pointer events and set touch-action where the canvas handles drags
Don't: Listen only for mouse events, leaving touch and pen input unhandled
Code Good: canvas.style.touchAction = 'none'; canvas.addEventListener('pointermove', updatePointer);
Code Bad: canvas.addEventListener('mousemove', updatePointer); // touch and pen input ignored

Description: Check window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') before auto-rotation, particle drift or camera movement; the preference asks for non-essential motion to be minimized. Reading .matches once at load is a snapshot, so attach a 'change' listener to keep the flag current if the OS setting changes mid-session.
Do: Use matchMedia.addEventListener('change') to keep noMotion reactive; gate all auto-animation on the live value
Don't: Read .matches once at startup and never update it — the scene ignores mid-session OS setting changes
Code Good: const mq = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)'); let noMotion = mq.matches; mq.addEventListener('change', e => { noMotion = e.matches; }); // In animate(): if (!noMotion) { mesh.rotation.y += dt * 0.8; particles.rotation.y += dt * 0.1; }
Code Bad: const noMotion = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches; // one-time snapshot — mid-session OS change is ignored entirely

Description: Add role='img' and a descriptive aria-label to renderer.domElement after appending it to the DOM. Screen readers receive no information from a WebGL canvas — the aria-label is the only description they can announce to users.
Do: Set role='img' and a meaningful aria-label on renderer.domElement before or after appending it
Don't: Append the canvas to the DOM with no accessibility attributes — invisible to screen readers
Code Good: renderer.domElement.setAttribute('role', 'img'); renderer.domElement.setAttribute('aria-label', 'Interactive 3D product viewer. Drag to rotate. Scroll to zoom.'); document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement);
Code Bad: document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement); // bare canvas — screen readers announce nothing

Guideline: Configure Loaded glTF Meshes by Traversal
Description: Loaded meshes keep Object3D defaults, so castShadow and receiveShadow are false. Traverse gltf.scene to set shadow flags or material overrides on each child Mesh before adding it.
Do: Import GLTFLoader from 'three/addons/' and traverse gltf.scene to configure child meshes
Don't: Add gltf.scene directly and expect it to cast or receive shadows
Code Good: import { GLTFLoader } from 'three/addons/loaders/GLTFLoader.js'; const gltf = await new GLTFLoader().loadAsync('model.glb'); gltf.scene.traverse((o) => { if (o.isMesh) { o.castShadow = true; o.receiveShadow = true; } }); scene.add(gltf.scene);
Code Bad: new GLTFLoader().load('model.glb', (gltf) => scene.add(gltf.scene)); // shadow flags stay false on every child

Description: THREE.LOD swaps between detail levels by camera distance so distant objects use cheaper geometry.
Do: Use THREE.LOD to reduce triangle count on distant objects automatically
Don't: Render the same high-polygon geometry for every object regardless of its distance from the camera
Code Good: const lod = new THREE.LOD(); lod.addLevel(highDetailMesh, 0); lod.addLevel(midDetailMesh, nearDistance); lod.addLevel(lowDetailMesh, farDistance); scene.add(lod);
Code Bad: scene.add(highDetailMesh); // full triangle cost at every distance

Description: Since r171 WebGPURenderer and node materials are imported from 'three/webgpu' and TSL from 'three/tsl'. WebGPURenderer uses WebGPU when available and otherwise falls back to a WebGL 2 backend. render() is only safe after initialization: render inside setAnimationLoop, or await renderer.init() for on-demand rendering.
Do: Import from 'three/webgpu' and render inside setAnimationLoop or after await renderer.init()
Don't: Call render() on a WebGPURenderer before it has initialized
Code Good: import * as THREE from 'three/webgpu'; const renderer = new THREE.WebGPURenderer({ antialias: true }); renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => renderer.render(scene, camera));
Code Bad: const renderer = new THREE.WebGPURenderer(); renderer.render(scene, camera); // not initialized yet
